content: Tendinitis refers to the inflammation, irritation, and swelling of a tendon, which is the fibrous tissue that connects muscle to bone. In many cases, tendinosis, which is the degeneration of the tendon, may also be present alongside tendinitis. The symptoms of tendinitis typically include pain and tenderness along the affected tendon, often near a joint. This pain may worsen at night or during movement and physical activity. Tendinitis can result from injury, repetitive overuse, or the natural aging process, as tendons lose their elasticity over time. It may also occur in individuals with systemic conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes. While tendinitis can affect any tendon, it is most commonly observed in the elbow, heel (Achilles tendinitis), shoulder, and wrist. Certain individuals are at higher risk of developing tendinitis, particularly those with systemic diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes. To diagnose tendinitis, a healthcare provider will conduct a physical examination, assessing for pain and tenderness when the muscle connected to the tendon is used against resistance. Specific diagnostic tests may be performed for particular tendons. The affected tendon may appear inflamed, and the skin overlying the tendon may feel warm or appear red. It is important to seek medical attention if symptoms of tendinitis develop. Early intervention can prevent complications and promote recovery. The primary goal of treatment is to alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. Resting or immobilizing the affected tendon is crucial for recovery, which may involve the use of a splint or removable brace. Applying heat or cold to the area can also provide relief. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin or ibuprofen, are effective in reducing both pain and inflammation. In some cases, corticosteroid injections into the tendon sheath may be administered to control pain and facilitate the initiation of physical therapy. Physical therapy is essential for stretching and strengthening the affected muscle and tendon, restoring proper function, promoting healing, and preventing future injuries. In rare cases, surgical intervention may be required to remove inflamed tissue surrounding the tendon. With appropriate treatment and rest, symptoms of tendinitis generally improve. If the condition is caused by repetitive overuse, modifying work or activity habits may be necessary to prevent recurrence. Potential complications of tendinitis include an increased risk of tendon rupture due to prolonged inflammation and the recurrence of symptoms.
